2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern / Not applicable for cross-sectional municipal indicators (complete census of all 84 municipalities in Hidalgo); however, longitudinal 2013-2022 tariff tracking in Table 4 is restricted to the 15-municipality CAASIM utility rather than all 84 municipalities.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High risk (uncontrolled): purely descriptive municipal ratios and aggregate time series with no statistical adjustment or stratification for municipal income distribution, informal sector earnings, household size heterogeneity around the 3.7 mean, rural spring/well self-supply, climate, or topography.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-strong doctrinal source identification (accurate citation of UN General Comment No. 15, UNGA Res. 64/292, Mexican Constitution Arts. 4 and 115, Ley de Aguas Nacionales, REPDA water-rights registry, and Hidalgo Periódico Oficial municipal tariff decrees 55-170 of 2022), but weak-to-moderate empirical operationalization because tariff-coding rules across heterogeneous municipal decrees are undocumented and formal REPDA legal concession volumes are conflated with actual physical household water delivery.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High risk: municipal per-capita water availability (DAmh) divides legally concessioned REPDA volumes by population without accounting for distribution leakage, unused concessions, or intermittent rationing (tandeo), yielding paradoxically high supply estimates in rural municipalities with high proportions of unpiped dwellings (e.g., Pacula 361 L/h/d with 23% unpiped; Huautla 122 L/h/d with 34.8%-36% unpiped). Affordability (GPAHmh) combines a uniform 2017 national bottled-water spending average (51.74 MXN/week) with imputed 1- and 2-minimum-wage incomes rather than observed municipal household spending and incomes, alongside denominator inconsistencies in Table 4.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate: relies on synthetic ecological/simulated household indicators (concessioned liters per inhabitant and simulated minimum-wage expenditure shares) and basin-level CONAGUA water-quality traffic lights rather than direct household-level measurement of tap-water continuity, potability, health outcomes, or out-of-pocket water expenditure.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern / Can't tell: no pre-registered protocol or analysis plan exists; municipal availability estimates are fully reported for all 84 municipalities (Tables 1-2), but municipality-specific tariff and expenditure figures are reported only as grouped map intervals (Map 4) rather than exact values, and internal numerical discrepancies on PDF pp. 10 and 16 (Table 4) are unacknowledged.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Low concern for cross-sectional municipal coverage (includes the complete administrative universe of all 84 municipalities in Hidalgo), but moderate concern for longitudinal affordability estimates (Table 4 uses only CAASIM tariffs covering 15 municipalities and a national rather than state/municipal bottled-water expenditure survey mean).

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: García Salazar and Lara Figueroa (2024) conduct a doctrinal-empirical compliance study evaluating the Human Right to Water (DHA) across all 84 municipalities of Hidalgo, Mexico. Doctrinally and contextually, the paper is strong: it accurately grounds its evaluation in international norms (UN General Comment No. 15, UNGA Res. 64/292), Mexican constitutional provisions (Arts. 4 and 115), federal water law (Ley de Aguas Nacionales, REPDA), and 2022 state-enacted municipal tariff decrees (decrees 55-170), while situating findings within Hidalgo's complex institutional reality (intermittent tandeo delivery, CAASIM intermunicipal management, and over a century of untreated ZMVM wastewater irrigation in the Mezquital Valley). Methodologically, however, its empirical operationalization exhibits major measurement, coding, and inferential limitations: per-capita water availability is proxied by legally concessioned REPDA volumes rather than actual water delivered to homes (ignoring leakage and tandeo rationing, producing paradoxically high availability in rural municipalities with high shares of unpiped dwellings); household affordability combines undocumented single-tariff extractions from municipal decrees with a uniform 2017 national bottled-water expenditure mean and hypothetical 1- or 2-minimum-wage incomes rather than observed household budgets; internal unit/denominator inconsistencies appear on p. 178 and in Table 4; and purely descriptive accounting cannot support causal claims or control for municipal socioeconomic and geographic confounding.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate-to-high concern (structured non-validated judgment: strong legal source accuracy, jurisdictional specificity, and institutional context, but weak measurement validity, coding transparency, confounding control, and causal identification)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid / descriptive municipal institutional-data compliance study evaluating Human Right to Water availability, quality, and affordability across all 84 municipalities of Hidalgo, Mexico
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design and objectives on [PDF Pages 1, 4 of 21] (pp. 169, 172); international and Mexican constitutional/statutory legal framework on [PDF Pages 4-7 of 21] (pp. 172-175); empirical data sources, algebraic formulas (DAmh, GPAHmh), and hypothesis in Materiales y métodos on [PDF Pages 7-8 of 21] (pp. 175-176); hydrological, water-quality, and institutional context on [PDF Pages 8-13 of 21] (pp. 176-181); municipal availability and affordability estimates (Tables 1-4, Map 4) on [PDF Pages 13-17 of 21] (pp. 181-185); policy conclusions and database URLs on [PDF Pages 17-21 of 21] (pp. 185-189).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study combines doctrinal analysis of international and Mexican Human Right to Water norms and municipal statutory tariff laws (Periódico Oficial decrees 55-170 of 2022; REPDA legal water-rights concessions) with purely descriptive municipal indicator accounting across Hidalgo's 84 municipalities. It fits none of the six conventional empirical checklists: there is no randomized assignment (RoB 2), no quasi-experimental intervention evaluation with a comparator group (ROBINS-I), no statistical association/regression analysis testing exposure-outcome relationships (ruling out JBI Analytical Cross Sectional and Cohort checklists), no primary qualitative fieldwork (CASP), no mixed-methods integration (MMAT), and no systematic literature search (AMSTAR 2). Accordingly, the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework is the exact matching instrument.
